articles.author: Marvin Ochieng
articles.description:
1. Forking a Repository
Click Fork (top right).
Clone your fork:
git clone <your-forked-url>
Work on your computer, then push changes to your fork.
Collaborating on GitHub

Assign tasks to people.
Push your code and open a pull request.
Review and discuss changes with teammates.
Communicate clearly in comments.
Creating a Pull Request

Make a new branch:
git checkout -b my-feature
Make and commit your changes:
git commit -m "what you changed"
Push your branch:
git push origin my-feature
On GitHub, click Compare & pull request.
Write a title and description, then submit.
Resolving Merge Conflicts
Pull latest code:
git pull origin main
If there are conflicts, fix them in the files.
Add and commit the fixed files.
Push again:
git push
Code Review
Check the pull request.
Review code for quality and clarity.
Leave helpful comments.
Approve or request changes.
Managing Issues
Open an issue with a title and details.
Label and assign it.
Comment updates.
Close it when done.
Basic Git Commands



git init # Start git in a folder

git clone <url> # Copy a repo

git status # Check changes

git add . # Stage changes

git commit -m "message" # Save changes

git pull # Update from remote

git push # Upload your changes

git checkout # b branch – New branch

git merge branch # Combine branches

Pushing Changes
Update your branch:
git pull origin main
Commit your changes:
git commit -m "message"

Push:
git push origin your-branch

Open or update a pull request.
articles.title: Day 2. Learning about Git and Git and Github

articles.author: Prasoon
articles.description:
Programming as an Art — with Meaning



✍️ By Prasoon Jadon

📖 A book about the emotions behind code, written at 16
"Code is not just logic. It's language. It's expression. It's us."
Explanation:

Programming isn’t just about instructions to a machine — it’s how we express our thoughts, our dreams, our creativity. Just like poetry or painting, code reflects who we are.
"Every bug I fix feels like a little battle I won against myself."
Explanation:

Debugging isn’t just technical — it’s emotional. You grow each time you solve something. The enemy isn’t the error… it's your own limits being pushed.
"We don’t write code to be robots. We write it to become more human."
Explanation:

Good code serves people. Behind every app or tool is a human need. And the better we understand people, the better we code.
"Even when no one claps, I keep building — because my code hears me."
Explanation:

You may not always get likes or praise. But creation itself is healing. It listens, responds, and grows with you. You don’t build for applause — you build for your soul.
"When I was too shy to speak, code became my voice."
Explanation:

For many introverts or creators, programming is their first form of self-expression. It gives confidence when words don’t come easily.
"Programming is the only art where silence means perfection."
Explanation:

In music, silence might be awkward. In code, no errors means everything is working — a silent program is a perfect one.
"The best code isn’t the most complex. It’s the most honest."
Explanation:

Writing clean, understandable code is a form of honesty. It means you care about others reading your work. Simplicity is strength.
📖 Read the full book here:

👉 Programming as an Art – by Prasoon Jadon
If any of these quotes touched you, I’d love to know in the comments.

You’re not just reading my book — you’re reading a piece of my heart.
— Prasoon
articles.title: 🧠 Quotes from *Programming as an Art* — with Meaning

articles.author: RazcoDev
articles.description:
A few weeks ago, I was helping a teammate debug something.

I shared my screen, opened VSCode, and without realizing —

my .env file was visible.
Right there, for 20+ seconds:
API_SECRET=sk_live_7b3c...
It wasn’t recorded, luckily. But it could’ve been.

And if it was a live demo, stream, or recorded tutorial…

💀 I’d be regenerating keys and praying no one used them.

We all know not to push secrets to Git.

But what about when you're:
Live coding
Sharing your browser
Recording a bug demo
Pair programming
Your screen becomes an attack surface — and you usually don’t realize it until after the fact.
After that moment, I found Entropy — a dev-focused Chrome extension that:
Detects secrets and tokens on your screen

Blurs them automatically

Even turns itself on when you're in a meeting
It’s like a DLP for your browser, made for developers.
If you ever screen share as a dev — even once — get Entropy.

It catches what your eyes miss.
🔗 Install Entropy
Ever leaked a secret on screen? Drop your horror story below 👇
articles.title: ⚠️ I Leaked an API Key While Screen Sharing. This Chrome Extension Would've Saved Me.
